intro: Mumbai's Gateway of India was built to welcome a king in 1911 and finished thirteen years later in 1924. It became the ceremonial door of the British Empire in India, and then, in February 1948, the door the Empire walked out of.
page_title: Gateway of India: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: In December 1911 King George V and Queen Mary landed at Apollo Bunder in Bombay, the first reigning British monarchs ever to visit India. They had come for the Delhi Durbar, but the city wanted a permanent mark of the landing. Governor Sir George Sydenham Clarke laid the foundation stone on 31 March 1911, before the design even existed. The Scottish architect George Wittet, Bombay's consulting architect, drew up an Indo-Saracenic triumphal arch; his final design was sanctioned in 1914. Reclamation of the harbor front took until 1919, construction ran from 1915, and on 4 December 1924 Viceroy Rufus Isaacs inaugurated the finished monument at a cost of Rs. 21.13 lakhs.
sections.heading: A door for an empire

sections.body: Wittet's design fuses Islamic, Hindu and European Gothic Revival elements, with the arch profile showing 16th-century Gujarati influence. The structure stands 26 meters high in yellow basalt stiffened with reinforced concrete, a special mix meant to survive the sea air. The central dome is 14.6 meters across and rises 25.3 meters. Four turrets with intricate carved latticework mark the corners. Stone jali screens filter the sunlight into geometric patterns on the inner walls. Flanking the great arch are large halls, each able to hold about 600 people. The whole monument stands on a high platform against tides and monsoon flooding, with steps at the rear descending to the Arabian Sea.
sections.heading: Yellow basalt and Gujarati arches

sections.body: For two decades the Gateway did the job it was built for: viceroys, governors and dignitaries arriving by sea passed through it as their ceremonial entrance to India. Then history reversed the traffic. After independence, the last British troops to leave India marched through the arch in a formal ceremony on 28 February 1948, the Somerset Light Infantry passing beneath the monument raised for the Empire's glory. The doorway built to announce British power became the exit it walked out of. Today the arch belongs to Mumbai: tourists, photographers, wedding parties, and the boats to Elephanta Island all gather in its shadow.
sections.heading: The empire's farewell

sections.body:
The monument has starred under its own name. Gateway of India (1957) is a Bombay noir built around the landmark: Madhubala plays a woman who flees gangsters and takes refuge in the crowds at the Gateway, with the climax unfolding around the monument itself. The film even booked its star a suite at the Taj, next door, for the midnight shoots.

Hollywood came calling when Christopher Nolan shot Tenet (2020) in Mumbai: the production filmed Robert Pattinson and Dimple Kapadia at the Gateway of India, on Colaba Causeway and around the Taj in 2019. Ritesh Batra's Photograph (2019) casts Nawazuddin Siddiqui as Rafi, a street photographer working the Gateway's tourist crowds, who talks a stranger into posing as his fiancee; the monument is practically a co-star. Rohit Shetty's Singham Returns (2014) made headlines as the first film shot at the Gateway after the 26/11 terror attacks, which had struck the neighboring Taj Mahal Palace Hotel. Earlier Bollywood used the arch as Mumbai shorthand too: Ghajini (2008) and Mann (1999) both staged scenes on its seafront promenade.

The arch's most reproduced real-life image is not from any film. On 28 February 1948 the cameras recorded the last British battalion marching out through the monument, drums beating, to the ships waiting in the harbor: the ceremonial end of the Raj, framed by the arch built to celebrate it.

timeline.text: King George V and Queen Mary land at Apollo Bunder, the first reigning British monarchs to visit India.
Governor Sir George Sydenham Clarke lays the foundation stone.
George Wittet's final Indo-Saracenic design is sanctioned.
Construction in yellow basalt and reinforced concrete; harbor reclamation completed 1919.
Viceroy Rufus Isaacs inaugurates the Gateway; cost Rs. 21.13 lakhs.
The film Gateway of India, starring Madhubala, is released.
The last British troops leave India, marching through the arch.
Singham Returns becomes the first film shot at the Gateway after the 26/11 attacks.
Christopher Nolan films Tenet scenes at the Gateway with Robert Pattinson and Dimple Kapadia.
